client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are next week and I honestly don't feel ready at all. I've been working so many hours at my part-time job just to cover rent that I barely have time to study, and it's like this constant knot in my stomach that won't go away. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the problem is just... real, you know? I don't have more hours in the day.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling that knot in your stomach — you're carrying a genuinely heavy load right now, balancing real financial pressure with academic demands, and I want you to know that stress is a completely understandable response to a truly difficult situation, not a sign that something is wrong with you. You're right that talking won't magically create more hours, but sometimes when we're overwhelmed, our minds make the situation feel even more unmanageable than it already is, and it can help to untangle what's *actually* in your control from what feels impossible. I'm curious — when you imagine the week ahead, what feels like the single most urgent or frightening piece of it for you?

client: Honestly, the most frightening thing is my statistics exam on Thursday, because I've barely touched the material and it's worth 40% of my grade. If I fail it, I could fail the whole course, and then I'd have wasted all this money and time, which just makes the anxiety spiral even worse. I guess what scares me most is that I don't even know where to start, so I end up just... freezing and not studying at all.
therapist: That freezing response makes so much sense — when something feels overwhelming and we don't know where to start, our brain can treat it like a threat and shut down, which then feeds the very spiral you're describing. I'd gently invite you to notice that thought "I don't even know where to start" — because that feeling of total lostness can make the mountain look much bigger than it actually is when broken into smaller steps. If you had to pick just *one* small, concrete thing you could look at in statistics tonight — even just for 20 minutes — what might that be?

client: I guess I could look at the practice exam my professor posted, just to see what topics are actually on it. But honestly, 20 minutes feels almost pointless when I have a week's worth of material to cover, and part of me thinks I'll just look at it, feel even more lost, and then feel worse than before I started. It's like, what if the small step just confirms that I'm already too far behind?
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense, but I want to gently point out that you're predicting a specific outcome — that looking at the practice exam *will* make you feel worse and confirm you're too far behind — and treating that prediction as a certainty, when really it's just one possible result. The other possibility is that you look at it and discover some topics you actually do know, or that the gaps feel more manageable than your anxious mind is currently imagining. What do you think it would mean about you if you looked at the practice exam and *did* find some things you recognized?

client: I guess if I found some things I recognized, it would mean I'm not completely hopeless, which... I don't know, that's actually kind of hard to imagine right now. My brain keeps defaulting to this idea that I've already failed before I've even tried, and I know logically that's not totally fair to myself. But even saying that out loud, I still feel like the odds are stacked against me with the job hours and everything, so one small win on a practice exam might not feel like enough to shake that feeling.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already see that thought — "I've already failed before I've even tried" — for what it is: not a fact, but a story your exhausted, stressed mind is telling you right now, and noticing that gap between the thought and reality is actually a genuine skill. You're right that one small win won't erase the very real pressures you're facing, but I wonder if you're holding yourself to an unfair standard where only a *complete* turnaround would count as progress. What would you say to a close friend who was in exactly your situation — same job pressure, same exam fear — if they told you they felt completely hopeless?

client: I'd probably tell a friend that they've been dealing with a really unfair situation and that struggling doesn't mean they're a failure. But it's so much easier to say that to someone else than to actually believe it for myself, which I know is kind of a cliche thing to say but it genuinely feels different when it's your own life on the line. I think part of me feels like I don't deserve that same compassion because I made the choice to take on so many work hours, so some part of me feels like this is just... my fault.
therapist: That belief — "I don't deserve compassion because I made this choice" — is such an important one to pause on, because it's essentially punishing you for making a decision you had to make just to keep a roof over your head, which isn't a character flaw, it's survival. Most people in your situation would have made the same choice, and struggling with the consequences doesn't cancel out your worthiness of kindness — including from yourself. I'm curious, where do you think that idea came from — that making a difficult trade-off means you forfeit the right to be gentle with yourself?

client: Honestly, I think it probably comes from how I grew up — my parents worked really hard and there wasn't a lot of room for excuses, so I internalized this idea that if things go wrong, you just push through and don't complain. Sitting here trying to trace it back feels a little strange, like I'm not sure how understanding where it came from actually helps me get through next Thursday. I guess I'm worried we're getting into territory that feels more abstract when what I really need is to figure out how to survive this week.
therapist: That's a really fair and self-aware redirect, and I want to honor it — understanding the roots of a belief is useful eventually, but you're right that right now you need something concrete to get through Thursday. So let's bring it back to this week: you mentioned looking at that practice exam as a possible first step, and I think that's actually a solid instinct. What would it take to protect even just a 30-minute window tonight to do exactly that — is there a realistic moment in your day where that could happen?

client: I get off work at 9pm tonight, so technically there's a window after that, but by then I'm usually so mentally drained that even scrolling my phone feels like effort. I could try to sit down with the practice exam then, but I'm genuinely worried I'll just stare at it blankly and then feel guilty for wasting the time instead of sleeping. I don't know, maybe that's just another excuse my brain is making, but the exhaustion after a shift is really real.
therapist: The exhaustion after a long shift is completely real, and I don't want you to dismiss that as an excuse — pushing yourself to study while genuinely depleted can sometimes backfire and reinforce that feeling of hopelessness. So rather than framing tonight as "study or fail," what if the only goal was just to *open* the practice exam, spend 10 minutes skimming the topics without any pressure to understand them, and then give yourself full permission to sleep? What feels more doable to you — trying that lighter version tonight, or is there a better window tomorrow where your mind might have a little more fuel?

client: The 10-minute version actually sounds less terrifying than what I was imagining, and I think I could probably do that tonight without it feeling like this huge commitment. But I'm a little skeptical of myself, honestly, because I have a habit of saying I'll do something small and then just not doing it when the moment actually comes. I guess I'm worried I'll get home, tell myself I deserve a break, and then wake up tomorrow feeling guilty that I didn't even try.
therapist: That self-awareness about your own patterns is actually really valuable — you're not just making a plan, you're honestly anticipating the obstacle, which puts you one step ahead. One thing that can help bridge the gap between intention and action is making the moment as frictionless as possible — so something like pulling up the practice exam on your phone *before* you leave work, so it's already open and waiting when you get home, rather than requiring a fresh decision when you're exhausted. What do you think gets in the way most in that moment — is it more that the motivation disappears, or that the effort of even starting feels like too much?

client: I think it's honestly both, but if I had to pick one, it's more that the motivation disappears — like, in the moment I just convince myself that one night won't matter and I'll make up for it tomorrow. The idea of pulling it up before I leave work is actually pretty smart, because it removes that decision point, but I'm still a little worried that I'll just close the tab and tell myself I'll look at it "in a minute" that never comes. I guess I'm just not sure I trust myself right now, and that's a weird feeling to sit with.
therapist: Not trusting yourself right now makes a lot of sense given how many times exhaustion has won out lately — that's not a character flaw, it's just a pattern that's been reinforced, and patterns can be changed with small, specific actions rather than willpower alone. One thing that might help is pairing the exam-opening with something you *already* do when you get home — like, the moment you sit down or take your shoes off, that's the trigger to glance at the screen for just 60 seconds before anything else. What's one thing you reliably do in the first few minutes of getting home that could serve as that anchor?

client: The first thing I always do is pour myself a glass of water and just stand in the kitchen for a minute, so I guess that could be the anchor point. It actually makes sense to tie it to that, because it's automatic enough that I don't have to think about it. I'm still a little nervous that even 60 seconds of looking at it will feel overwhelming and spiral into that frozen feeling, but I think the water thing is concrete enough that I might actually try it tonight.
therapist: That's a genuinely solid plan — water, kitchen, 60 seconds of just *looking*, no pressure to understand or solve anything yet, just to see what's there. And if you do feel that frozen feeling creep in, I want you to remember that you can close the tab and still count tonight as a win, because showing up at all when you're this exhausted and scared is not nothing. How will you know tomorrow morning whether tonight felt like a small step forward, even if it was just those 60 seconds?
